digo_source: Pakia (2005) App. III; Maundu & Tengnäs 2005 (Mdungu, Mudhungu)

teaser.en: Its trunk is studded with corky knobs, each tipped with a prickle, and its crushed leaves smell of lemon.

summary.en: *Mdungu*, the knobwood, is a spiny tree of dry bushland and coastal thicket with corky, prickle-tipped knobs on its trunk. It is a popular Digo medicine, boiled for malaria, and also gives a spice, a tea and toothbrushes.

about.en:
*Mdungu* is a spiny tree up to about 8 metres. Its trunk carries large corky knobs, each tipped with a sharp prickle, which make it one of the easiest trees in the bush to recognise.

The leaves are compound and smell of lemon when crushed, a sign of the citrus family it belongs to. The small round fruits ripen red and split open to show shiny black seeds.

where.en: It grows in dry bushland and coastal thicket. Look for its knobbly trunk at the edge of bush paths.

uses.en:
The root bark is boiled as a remedy for malaria, and Pakia records it as a popular general medicine among the Digo.

The fruits and leaves are used as a spice and to make tea, and its twigs are chewed as toothbrushes.

names.en: Pakia records the Digo names *mdungu* and *mjafari*; Maundu and Tengnäs give *mdungu* and *mudhungu*. In Swahili it is *mjafari*. Giriama speakers say *mudhungu* or *mjafari*, and Chonyi speakers *mdungu*. In English it is knobwood, and its scientific name is *Zanthoxylum chalybeum*.

reason.en: Same citrus family; its root bark is also boiled for malaria
Another tree used by the Digo for malaria
